acquisition.why: SEO is inbound and legal. Agents can do keyword research and page generation. Ranking is slow and fragile under Google updates and AI Overviews [E].

onboarding.why: Anonymous visitors. There is nothing to onboard.

delivery.why: Programmatic or AI-built pages plus data refreshes. Agents can maintain them, with human spot-checks for accuracy and affiliate disclosures.

billing.why: Ad networks and affiliate programmes pay out automatically.

support.why: Minimal: occasional contact-form emails and listing corrections.

scores.R_why: Cheap to build within £300 if Ricardo avoids premium domains (the $7k domain in the source is irrelevant). It fits 6-8 h/week. Income is slow, though: the cited example makes about $767/month after years. UK affiliate programmes (Amazon UK, Awin) exist. ASA/CMA disclosure is needed.
scores.M_why: Informational niches are heavily commoditised by AI content and squeezed by AI Overviews. Many people are copying the same 'vibe-coded directory' playbook. Some headroom remains in data-rich UK niches with tools such as calculators and filters [E].
scores.one_line: Highly automatable and legal, but there are zero first-hand income claims, the examples are demos or small earners, and Google/AI-Overview risk makes it a slow, low-ceiling bet [E].

acquisition.why: The proven case (Avenue) relied on door-to-door selling, which Ricardo can't do and agents can't automate. Paid social lead ads are legal but untested and costly to run against Calendly and Fresha. Cold email works only for trades set up as limited companies; most UK trades are sole traders, so PECR blocks it.

onboarding.why: A self-serve embed is possible, but local trades usually need hand-holding to install the widget and connect Google Business.

delivery.why: Multi-tenant SaaS runs unattended once it is stable. It still needs security and uptime monitoring.

support.why: Non-technical SMB customers generate frequent support requests, and bookings are business-critical, so failures escalate.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build the software, but the UK market has many established tools (Calendly, Fresha, Setmore, Square, Booksy, Jobber), several of them free. The AUD 85k/month case is founder-funded and sales-led with a full team. Paid ads to acquire SMBs would burn through £300 quickly. SMS features add PECR and Twilio cost complexity.
scores.M_why: Saturated, with free incumbents. Vibe-coded clones are trivially easy to make, so differentiation is close to nil.
scores.one_line: The real revenue evidence comes from in-person sales Ricardo can't replicate. Self-serve booking widgets are a crowded, free-incumbent market with heavy SMB support.

acquisition.why: Organic TikTok and app-store discovery are legal inbound channels. Agents can produce clips, but virality is luck-driven and depends on the platform.

delivery.why: An API wrapper running unattended. Ricardo still needs to monitor content safety.

billing.why: Stripe or app-store in-app purchases with credits.

support.why: Mostly refund and quality complaints. These can be templated.

scores.R_why: Technically trivial for Ricardo and cheap to test under £300. UK GDPR applies to face photos, which are biometric-adjacent. Image IP and the Online Safety Act/deepfake risk require moderation. Success depends on virality more than effort.
scores.M_why: ChatGPT and Gemini do this natively for free. Copycats appear the same day. These are fads with very short lifespans.
scores.one_line: Fully automatable and cheap to try, but it is a lottery ticket that frontier AI apps commoditise. The $10k/2-month claim dates from an earlier, less saturated window.

acquisition.why: Marketplace listings (Shopify, Chrome, WordPress, Excel/AppSource) provide inbound demand. Agents can optimise listings and answer reviews. Ricardo depends on the platform's ranking.

onboarding.why: One-click install via OAuth. Occasional setup questions.

delivery.why: Hosted software. Platform API changes need developer attention, which agents can mostly handle with Ricardo approving.

billing.why: Platform billing APIs (Shopify Billing) or Stripe.

support.why: Merchants expect responsive support, and review scores depend on it. Agents can handle the first line.

scores.R_why: Best fit for Ricardo's technical skills and his hours. Build costs are mostly time; platform fees are small (for example, $19 Shopify Partner dev is free, Chrome $5). There is no physical work, and selling to UK and global merchants is fine.
scores.M_why: Major marketplaces are crowded, and platforms absorb features (for example, Copilot in Excel). Narrow niches remain in smaller or newer marketplaces such as GoHighLevel, HubSpot and Zoom, and in long-tail gaps found through reviews [E].
scores.one_line: Strong structural fit (inbound marketplace demand, automatable SaaS), but all the income figures are hypothetical. Success hinges on picking an underserved niche in a niche marketplace [E].

acquisition.why: Local SEO with schema is inbound. Ricardo competes against Tripadvisor, Google Maps and AI answers. Selling sponsored listings is passive inbound or cold email to Ltd restaurants.

onboarding.why: Users need no onboarding. Sponsors can use a self-serve listing form.

delivery.why: Data must be kept current (closures, hours). Agents can refresh it but need human accuracy checks. Aggregating Google reviews carries terms-of-service risk.

billing.why: Ads are automatic. Sponsored listings can go through Stripe.

support.why: Restaurant correction and removal requests, plus disputes about AI-summarised reviews.

scores.R_why: Cheap to build, but London dining is dominated by Google Maps, Tripadvisor, Time Out, Hot Dinners and HappyCow. AI-aggregated reviews raise defamation, DMCC fake-review and Google terms-of-service issues. Restaurant sponsorship needs sales effort. No monetisation was shown.
scores.M_why: Saturated, with deep-pocketed incumbents. AI search answers 'best X near me' directly.
scores.one_line: Low-cost to build but faces incumbent and AI-answer dominance and legal risk around review aggregation. Revenue figures are third-party estimates or nonexistent.

acquisition.why: Discovery happens inside the ElevenLabs voice library. This is fully platform-dependent and needs no outreach.

delivery.why: Ricardo records once (a human task, about an hour), then ElevenLabs serves the voice.

scores.R_why: Nearly free, takes a few hours, and is available in the UK. A UK English accent may be a niche advantage [E]. The downside is reputational risk from misuse of Ricardo's voice. It is a side income, not a business.
scores.M_why: The library holds thousands of voices, and payouts concentrate in the top voices. Synthetic voices reduce demand for clones [E].
scores.one_line: A trivial, zero-cost passive experiment worth an afternoon, but earnings are unproven (no first-hand claims) and likely tens of pounds a month, not a scalable business [E].

acquisition.why: SEO is inbound. Agents can research and publish. Google updates, Helpful Content, Site Reputation Abuse rules and AI Overviews make results volatile.

delivery.why: AI drafting plus programmatic pages. Ricardo needs to fact-check and review quality to avoid spam penalties.

scores.R_why: Building from scratch fits £300 and 6-8 h/week. Buying a site like those in the examples ($10-22k) is far beyond budget. Premium ad networks need traffic thresholds. The 'Google update killed my sites' warning comes from first-hand experience.
scores.M_why: Mass AI-generated content and AI Overviews have hollowed out informational SEO. Data-driven programmatic niches (UK-specific specs or calculators) retain some room [E].
scores.one_line: The most-corroborated idea here and highly automatable, but 2026 search economics are hostile. It is viable only as a cheap, data-driven UK niche experiment with patient expectations [E].

acquisition.why: Cold email to agencies (limited companies) is PECR-OK. Agents can scrape prospects and produce sample remade ads. Ricardo still needs to check the samples, and response rates are uncertain.

onboarding.why: Self-serve web app, with possible demo calls for agencies.

delivery.why: A software wrapper on image APIs.

support.why: Agencies expect quality tweaks and brand consistency. Agents can handle most of this.

scores.R_why: The build is easy, but agencies already have Canva, Adobe Firefly, AdCreative.ai, Meta Advantage+ and direct ChatGPT/Gemini access. Remaking clients' ads uses brand IP without permission. Unlimited plans carry API cost risk.
scores.M_why: Very crowded and funded category. Ad platforms bundle generative creative for free.
scores.one_line: Legal B2B cold email and automatable delivery, but a thin wrapper in a market saturated by funded tools and free platform features. Evidence is a single suggestion with no revenue.
